title: THYROID EYE DISEASE: THE DEFINITIVE CLINICAL COMPENDIUM
summary: Thyroid eye disease (TED), or Graves ophthalmopathy, is the most common cause of adult proptosis and stems from a complex organ-specific autoimmune reaction. This guide covers the pathogenesis, EUGOGO classification, clinical manifestations from lid retraction to sight-threatening optic neuropathy, and the multi-staged medical and surgical management protocols.

data.title: THYROID EYE DISEASE: THE DEFINITIVE CLINICAL COMPENDIUM
data.summary: Thyroid eye disease (TED), or Graves ophthalmopathy, is the most common cause of adult proptosis and stems from a complex organ-specific autoimmune reaction. This guide covers the pathogenesis, EUGOGO classification, clinical manifestations from lid retraction to sight-threatening optic neuropathy, and the multi-staged medical and surgical management protocols.

sections.title: Introduction & Thyrotoxicosis
sections.content: Thyroid eye disease (TED), also known as thyroid-associated orbitopathy and Graves ophthalmopathy, is a common orbital disorder and is the most common cause of both bilateral and unilateral proptosis in an adult. Thyrotoxicosis (hyperthyroidism) is a condition involving excessive secretion of thyroid hormones. Graves disease, the most common form of hyperthyroidism, is an autoimmune disorder in which IgG antibodies bind to receptors in the thyroid gland and stimulate secretion of thyroid hormones. It is more common in females and may be associated with other autoimmune disorders.

rows: Presentation often in the fourth or fifth decades; more common in females.
Weight loss despite good appetite, increased bowel frequency, sweating, heat intolerance, nervousness, irritability, palpitations, weakness and fatigue.
Enlargement of the thyroid gland (goitre), tremor, palmar erythema and warm and sweaty skin.
Thyroid acropachy: Similar to clubbing of the fingers (1%). Pretibial myxoedema (1–5%): Indurated thickening of the skin of the shins.
Other autoimmune disorders can be associated.

sections.title: Thyroid Function & Management
content: 1. Initial Testing: TSH level (Commonly tested initially).
2. Secondary Investigation: If TSH is low, or normal but disease is suspected, carry out additional investigations.
3. Treatment Options: Carbimazole, propylthiouracil, propranolol, thyroid ablation with radioactive iodine, and partial thyroidectomy.

sections.title: Risk Factors - Extended Detail
sections.content: Once a patient has Graves disease, the major clinical risk factor for developing TED is smoking. The greater the number of cigarettes smoked per day, the greater the risk and giving up smoking seems to reduce the risk. Women are five times more likely to be affected by TED than men, but this largely reflects the increased incidence of Graves disease in women. Radioactive iodine used to treat hyperthyroidism can worsen TED. This condition can also, though less commonly, occur in euthyroid and hypothyroid (including treated hyperthyroid) patients. It can sometimes be the presenting manifestation of thyroid-related disease.

branches: Autoimmune: Anti-thyrotropin-receptor antibody reacts against thyroid cells and orbital fibroblasts.
Receptors: Upregulation of Insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF-1R) and TSH receptor (TSHR) in orbital/brow fat.
Inflammation: Extraocular muscles, interstitial tissues, orbital fat, and lacrimal glands affected.
Muscle Swelling: Muscles can swell up to eight times normal size due to glycosaminoglycan secretion and osmotic water imbibition.
Lipogenesis: Induced by fibroblasts and preadipocytes causing fat enlargement.
Fibrosis: Degeneration leads to fibrosis, causing restrictive myopathy and diplopia.

rows: Eyes are red and painful. Tends to remit within 1–3 years.
Eyes are white; painless motility defects may be present.
(1) Soft tissue involvement, (2) Lid retraction, (3) Proptosis, (4) Optic neuropathy, (5) Restrictive myopathy.
Only about 10% of patients develop serious long-term ocular problems.

sections.title: EUGOGO Classification (2021)
content: ACTIVITY ASSESSMENT:
• Spontaneous retrobulbar pain.
• Pain on attempted upward or downward gaze.
• Redness of eyelids.
• Redness of conjunctiva.
• Swelling of conjunctiva or plica.
• Swelling of eyelids.
• Chemosis.
SEVERITY ASSESSMENT:
• Mild: Minor impact on daily life.
• Moderate–severe: Moderate–severe soft tissue involvement, lid retraction ≥ 2 mm, diplopia, and proptosis ≥ 3 mm.
• Sight-threatening: Due to optic neuropathy or corneal breakdown.

sections.title: Soft Tissue Involvement
content: Symptoms: Grittiness, red eyes, lacrimation, photophobia, puffy lids, and retrobulbar discomfort.
Epibulbar hyperaemia: Sensitive sign of activity; focal hyperaemia outlines horizontal recti insertions.
Periorbital swelling: Caused by oedema and infiltration; associated with chemosis and fat prolapse.
Tear insufficiency: Common instability of the tear film.
Corneal signs: Punctate epithelial erosions, superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis, bacterial keratitis, thinning, and scarring.

sections.title: Lid Retraction Signs
content: Prevalence: Occurs in 50% of Graves patients.
Mechanism: Müller muscle overstimulation, levator/inferior rectus fibrosis, and secondary overaction.
Dalrymple sign: Lid retraction/spasm in primary gaze (widened palpebral opening).
Kocher sign: Staring and frightened appearance on attentive fixation.
von Graefe sign: Retarded descent of the upper lid on downgaze (lid lag).
Scleral Show: Margin is level with or above superior limbus; lower margin is below inferior limbus.

sections.title: Proptosis & Restrictive Myopathy
content: PROPTOSIS: Axial, unilateral/bilateral, symmetrical/asymmetrical, and frequently permanent. Severe cases lead to exposure keratopathy and corneal ulceration.
MYOPATHY: 30–50% develop ophthalmoplegia. Restricted by inflammatory oedema then fibrosis. Causes double vision and discomfort.
Order of Rectus Involvement (Approximate):
1. Inferior Rectus (Elevation defect) - Most common motility deficit.
2. Medial Rectus (Abduction defect) - May simulate sixth nerve palsy.
3. Superior Rectus (Depression defect).
4. Lateral Rectus (Adduction defect).

sections.title: Optic Neuropathy: SIGHT THREATENING
content: Occurs in up to 6% of patients.
Caused by compression of optic nerve or blood supply at the orbital apex by enlarged recti.
Scleral show/proptosis may be ABSENT while nerve compression is present.
Symptom: Impairment of central vision. Patients should self-monitor by occluding eyes and assessing color intensity (e.g., TV screen).
Signs: Reduced Visual Acuity (VA), Colour desaturation, diminished light brightness appreciation.
Critical Sign: Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) gives cause for marked concern.
Field Defects: Central or paracentral, may be combined with nerve fibre bundle defects (confusable with glaucoma).
Optic Disc: Normal, swollen, or rarely atrophic.

sections.title: Investigations & Imaging
content: Visual field testing: For suspected optic nerve compromise or baseline.
Imaging (MRI, CT, Ultrasound): Indicated for equivocal diagnosis or pre-surgery.
Radiological Pattern: Muscle belly enlargement with tendon sparing.
Visual Evoked Potentials (VEP): Utilized in some optic neuropathy cases.

sections.title: Treatment Choice Factors
content: Treatment depends on: (a) Clinical activity, (b) Severity, (c) Duration.
Anti-inflammatory efficacy: Significantly less effective after 18 months duration.
Cessation of smoking: The first measure in ALL cases.
Radioiodine precaution: Give short course oral steroids if TED is pre-existing.

sections.title: Management of Mild & Active Disease
content: Lubricants: For SLK, corneal exposure, and dryness.
Topical Agents: Steroids, NSAIDs, or ciclosporin.
Selenium: Sodium selenite 200 μg daily for 6 months (in deficient areas).
Postural adjustment: Head elevation with three pillows during sleep.
Eyelid taping: During sleep to alleviate mild exposure keratopathy.

sections.title: Moderate–Severe Active Disease: Steroids
content: 1. Clinical Activity Score (CAS): Calculate based on EUGOGO; Treat if score ≥ 3/7.
2. Oral Steroids: Prednisolone 60–80 mg/day initially, then tapered.
3. IV Methylprednisolone: Better tolerability and superior outcomes vs oral. Regimen: 0.5 g once weekly for 6 weeks, then 0.25 g once weekly for 6 weeks.
4. Monitoring: Max response in 2–8 weeks; discontinue oral therapy after several months if possible.
5. Contraindications (IV): Hepatic dysfunction, significant CVD, uncontrolled hypertension, or diabetes.

sections.title: Advanced Medical Therapies
content: Combined Therapy: IV corticosteroids weekly + Mycophenolate sodium (0.72 g/day for 24 weeks) is the regimen of choice.
Orbital steroid injections: Triamcinolone acetate (less effective than systemic).
Low-dose fractionated radiotherapy: Second-line. 40% non-response rate. Risks: cataract, radiation retinopathy, local cancer.
Combined Irradiation: Radiotherapy + Azathioprine + Low-dose prednisolone.
Second-line Monoclonals: Rituximab, Tocilizumab.
Teprotumumab: IGF-1R inhibitor; effective for proptosis/CAS in acute and chronic TED; risk of hearing loss.

sections.title: Management of Acute Sight-Threatening TED
content: Aggressive Treatment: Pulsed IV methylprednisolone (0.5–1 g for 3 days or alternate days).
Dose Limit: Keep cumulative dose below 8 g to reduce liver risk.
Surgical Intervention: Orbital wall/apex decompression if steroids are ineffective (20%) or contraindicated.
Adjuvants: Orbital radiotherapy.
Mandatory Monitoring: Liver function tests, gastric protection, and osteoporosis prophylaxis.

rows: 1. Orbital Decompression → 2. Strabismus Surgery → 3. Eyelid Surgery.

One-wall (lateral): 4-5 mm reduction. Two-wall (medial/lateral): Balanced but risk of diplopia. Three-wall (+floor): 6-10 mm reduction; risk of hypoglobus/nerve damage. Four-wall (+roof): For very severe cases.
Requires stable deviation for 6–12 months. Goal: Binocular vision in primary/reading gaze. RECESSION ONLY (never resect). Adjustable sutures preferred.
Mild: Müllerotomy. Severe: Recession/disinsertion of levator aponeurosis/suspensory ligament. Lower lid: Recession of retractors +/- hard palate graft.
Temporary measure for lid retraction (levator/Müller) or diplopia while awaiting surgery.

content.explanation: T: Tendon Sparing (in imaging). E: EUGOGO (score for activity). D: Decompression (for sight-threat). P: Pulsed Steroids (first line for neuropathy). R: Recession only (no resection in muscles). I: Immunosuppression (prevent long-term complications). N: No Smoking (first measure). C: Cumulative Steroids (stay < 8g). I: IGF-1R Inhibitors (Teprotumumab). P: Pillows (3 for head elevation). L: Lid lag (von Graefe sign). E: Elevation defect (most common myopathy). S: Scleral show (sign of retraction).
